_comment: The quality bar for the property-concierge agent, as code.
scripts/prompt_gate.py runs the property-concierge-eval dataset (18 items)
against a prompt version and exits non-zero if any run-level mean falls
below its threshold here. This file is the artifact to show a customer when
they ask 'what stops a bad prompt reaching production?' — the answer is a
reviewable file in git, not a person remembering to check a dashboard.
THESE NUMBERS ARE DERIVED FROM MEASUREMENT, NOT TASTE. Measured on Claude
(claude-sonnet-4-6), 18 items, 2026-07-30. Note the two PRODUCTION columns:
that is the SAME prompt run twice, which is what makes this table useful.
metric                 first-draft  production  production(repeat)  candidate
avg-used-search-tool       1.000       1.000          1.000           1.000
avg-grounded-listings      1.000       1.000          1.000           1.000
avg-location-match         1.000       1.000          1.000           1.000
avg-budget-adherence       0.944       1.000          1.000           1.000
avg-language-match         0.833       1.000          1.000           1.000
avg-helpfulness            0.904       0.889          0.919           0.909
avg-groundedness           0.943       0.924          0.949           0.929
Read that table carefully, because it is the whole argument for how this
file is shaped.
1. THE CODE EVALUATORS ARE REPRODUCIBLE AND DECISIVE. Identical across all
three good runs, and they cleanly isolate the naive prompt's two real
defects: over-budget suggestions and answering Spanish in English.
2. THE JUDGES CANNOT TELL THESE PROMPTS APART. Running the SAME production
prompt twice moved judge means by up to 0.041 (relevance 0.892 -> 0.933).
That run-to-run swing is LARGER than every prompt-to-prompt judge delta in
the table. first-draft's judge scores (0.904 / 0.889 / 0.943) land INSIDE
production's own two-run range on all three metrics.
So a judge number here tells you which run you happened to look at, not
which prompt is better. Grade these three prompts on helpfulness and you
would conclude nothing at best, and something false at worst.
Hence: gate HARD on the deterministic code evaluators. Gate LOOSELY on judges
— they are a smoke alarm for catastrophic drops, not a ruler for 2-point
differences. A tight judge threshold would produce flaky builds AND could
block a correct fix on a bad roll.
Caveat for demos: `avg-language-match` (0.833 vs a 1.0 bar) is the reliable
blocker for the first-draft prompt. `avg-budget-adherence` fails by a thin
margin (0.944 vs 0.95) and may pass on some runs — the gate still goes red
either way, but do not promise which two rows will be flagged.
The code-eval thresholds of 1.0 leave production zero margin. That is
deliberate: a wrong-language answer or a hallucinated listing is a defect,
not a budget to spend. It does mean one genuinely bad item turns CI red —
which is the point.
